items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Like, I'll never forget the time I went to work with Johnny Detroit, one of the old New Orleans trumpet players who was a very fine musician.

ctx.x: Well, it's been pointed out, I think, in that book that just came out on Biggs, that a lot of solo passages he managed to create. And they only could have been created by someone who played by ear. Sure. Because he went off on a note, for instance, that a person who read, a well-trained red musician, would have thought it was a mistake and completely stopped the solo. Yeah. But Biggs managed to go on because he didn't have that reading novel. So it actually worked to his best.

And this is true of many of the people who have studied music. Like, I have people come up right now and tell me, you know, I'm playing something. And they say, how long did you study? I say, oh, I actually studied about six months. I said, six months? I studied ten years. I can't play anything, you know? They said, all I can do is when I got the notes there, you know, I can play it. But when they take the music away from me, I can't play it. Well, that's what the old musicians in New Orleans used to avoid. They…
